name: Galileo
first: First spacecraft to orbit Jupiter; atmospheric probe into Jupiter clouds
dispatch: Galileo should have been crippled before it even arrived. Its main antenna stuck half-open on the way to Jupiter, cutting its data rate to a trickle — and the mission succeeded anyway, because engineers rewrote its software from Earth to squeeze the science through a tiny backup antenna. It became the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, dropped a probe into the giant planet’s clouds, and spent eight years touring the moons. Its greatest find emerged slowly from that persistence: the way Jupiter’s magnetic field wrapped around Europa could only be explained by a salty ocean beneath the ice — the strongest case yet that a moon of Jupiter might hold liquid water, and life. At the end it was flown into Jupiter on purpose, so it could never fall onto Europa and contaminate it.
description: Launched from Space Shuttle Atlantis after the long post-Challenger pause, Galileo braved the inner asteroid belt and conducted the first long-term study of Jupiter and its moons from orbit. It discovered Europa's induced magnetic field — strong evidence of a subsurface ocean — and watched Shoemaker-Levy 9 slam into Jupiter. The mission ended with a controlled plunge into Jupiter in 2003 to avoid contaminating icy moons that might harbour conditions for life.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: STS-34 deploys Galileo and an inertial upper stage from Atlantis.

events.label: JUPITER ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Main engine burn captures Galileo into orbit; decades of moon science begin.
